intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant Parkinson disease-8 (PARK8) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding leucine-rich repeat kinase-2 (LRRK2) on chromosome 12q12.

paragraphs.text: Parkinson disease-8 (PARK8) is an autosomal dominant, usually late-onset parkinsonism that resembles idiopathic Parkinson disease (PD). Features include bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor and impaired postural reflexes, with a good response to levodopa (Wszolek et al., 1995; Zimprich et al., 2004). The neuropathology is pleomorphic. Brainstem dopaminergic degeneration has been accompanied by Lewy body PD, diffuse Lewy body disease, nigral degeneration without distinctive histopathology, or progressive supranuclear palsy-like pathology (Zimprich et al., 2004).

paragraphs.text: Wszolek et al. (1995) studied a family (family D) from western Nebraska whose ancestors probably came to the United States from England. The pedigree had 188 individuals across 6 generations, 18 of them affected, with autosomal dominant inheritance. Affected members developed typical levodopa-responsive PD with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor and impaired postural reflexes. There were no eye movement abnormalities, pyramidal or cerebellar signs, sensory disturbances, or orthostatic blood pressure changes, and the disease progressed slowly. PET with 18F-6-fluoro-L-dopa (FD) in 1 affected person showed decreased FD uptake in a pattern consistent with PD. Autopsy of another showed neuronal and pigmentary loss, gliosis and Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra pars compacta.

paragraphs.text: Hasegawa and Kowa (1997) reported autosomal dominant PD in 5 generations of a family living in Sagamihara City, Japan. The clinical features did not differ from common PD, but the neuropathology did. In autopsied cases, loss of melanin-containing cells was mild to moderate, the number of locus ceruleus neurons was maintained, and no Lewy bodies were found in any region where they frequently appear in PD. Funayama et al. (2005) later stated that the Sagamihara family was the family used to define the PARK8 locus. They described its pathology as pure nigral degeneration without Lewy bodies.

paragraphs.text: Lee et al. (2010) found that overexpression of LRRK2 G2019S in primary cortical neurons caused neurite shortening and cell death, whereas kinase-dead versions were not toxic. agent.process_note: I opened every file. I read in full all the abstracts and the full texts of Alcalay 2009, Alcalay 2010, Gehrke 2010 and Lee 2010. In Koch 2026 I searched for LRRK2 and Parkinson disease and read that section. Four papers were title only (Lesage 2005, Zhu 2006, Lesage 2008, Bandmann and Cookson 2012), so I used no more than their titles. Two papers were not cited. Girling 1993 is about DP-1/E2F, not this disorder. Koch 2026 concerns homozygous LRRK2 loss of function and kidney disease, not PARK8. The Dächsel review, the Lesage 2008 dyskinesia title and the Bandmann and Cookson commentary title were also left uncited. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so no gene MIM number is given. The chromosome location (12q12) comes from Satake 2009. Funayama 2005 does not name the kinase-domain missense mutation in its abstract, so that variant is not listed. Paisán-Ruíz 2004 does not use the symbol LRRK2 in its abstract; Alcalay 2009 links dardarin to LRRK2. Alcalay 2010 gives 35 G2019S carriers in the abstract and 31 in the results; Table 2 shows 4 further carriers who also had a second mutation, and the entry reports both figures. Marras 2011 found tremor was a more common presenting feature, while Alcalay 2009 found lower tremor scores in early-onset carriers; both are reported.
